title: Old Delhi's Sugar Toys: The Diwali Treats That Refuse to Disappear
excerpt: In Chandni Chowk's Batashe Wali Gali, columnist Vernika Awal finds artisans still crafting cheeni ke khilone and kheel-batashe — the fragile sugar offerings at the heart of a traditional Diwali puja.
body:
• Cheeni ke khilone — handcrafted sugar toys — and kheel-batashe (puffed rice and sugar drops) remain the ritual core of a traditional Diwali puja in Old Delhi.
  • In the Punjabi tradition columnist Vernika Awal describes, a tiny sugar hut sits atop a mound of kheel strewn with batashe, and the batashe are handed out as the first prasad.
  • In Chandni Chowk's Batashe Wali Gali, 73-year-old artisan Gurbachan Singh still makes the sugar toys — but says health-conscious buyers purchase fewer of them.
  • For diaspora families celebrating Diwali on November 8, the offering needs nothing elaborate: kheel and batashe presented to Goddess Lakshmi, as households have done for generations.

Long before the boxed mithai and velvet-wrapped gift hampers, Diwali in Old Delhi smelled of boiling sugar. In a column for Indulge Express, food columnist Vernika Awal describes how, as Dussehra fades and Diwali draws close, the lanes of Khari Baoli and Chandni Chowk fill with cheeni ke khilone — delicate handcrafted sugar toys — and kheel-batashe, the pairing of puffed roasted rice and airy sugar drops that sits at the centre of the festival's puja.

A Sugar Shop Inside the Puja

Awal recalls two Diwali kitchens. In her grandparents' home, the family rolled out namak paare and shaped laddus, but her favourite ritual was the market trip to buy sugar huts, kheel and batashe. In her relatives' Punjabi household in East Delhi, the tradition has a name: cheeni di hatti, literally "the sugar shop." During the Diwali puja, a tiny sugar toy shaped like a rustic hut is placed on top of a mountain of kheel strewn with batashe — and as a child, she writes, the great anticipation was waiting for those batashe to be handed out as the first divine prasad.

The pairing is not decorative. Food site Slurrp's account of lost Diwali food traditions notes that kheel, a form of puffed rice, is an integral part of Lakshmi Pujan on Diwali day, with batashe — small, flattened bites of sugar — placed at the altar and beside lit diyas to promote food security and the growth of the house. The timing is agricultural: Diwali falls at the Kharif harvest, at the end of the monsoon around October–November, which is what brings fresh rice and sugar to the festival table.

Harvest Sugar, Offered First

Awal traces the batasha's history to the era when sugarcane was a prized commodity along ancient trade routes, its juice transformed into what was essentially white gold. Because the autumn harvest aligns with the festival season, the confections became auspicious: batashe dipped in ghee are offered to deities during Navratri, and the first harvest of kheel and batashe is offered to Goddess Lakshmi to bless the home with abundance. The sugar toy, in other words, is a harvest offering before it is a sweet.

"Humara bachpan beeta hai in meethe khilono ke saath. Inke bina Diwali adhoori hai." (My childhood was spent with these sweet toys. Diwali remains incomplete without them.)

— A customer at Gurbachan Singh's stall, Chandni Chowk, quoted by Vernika Awal

The Artisan of Batashe Wali Gali

The craft survives in Batashe Wali Gali, the Old Delhi lane named for the sweet. There, Awal spoke with Gurbachan Singh, a 73-year-old artisan whose family has crafted the edible sugar toys for generations in a small corner of Chandni Chowk. Asked how times have changed, he was candid: "Logo ko cheeni se dar lagta hai ab, toh kam khareedte hain yeh khilone" — people are more conscious of sugar consumption now, so fewer of them buy these toys. Around his stall, the market tells the other half of the story: artisanal, presentation-ready mithai in velvet boxes, against which the plain white sugar huts stand as quiet survivors.

Yet the customers who do come are not buying a sweet; they are buying continuity. The elderly customer Awal quotes, selecting his treats at Singh's stall, put the tradition's survival in one line: "Jab tak hum hain, yeh hain" — these will stay alive as long as we keep them alive.

Keeping the Offering at Home

That is also the practical lesson for diaspora households celebrating Diwali this Sunday, November 8. The kheel-batashe offering asks for no specialist skill: puffed rice and sugar drops, a sugar khilona if you can find one, presented to Lakshmi before the sweets are shared as prasad. Slurrp places kheel and batashe among the Diwali traditions now taking a back seat to fusion treats and catered parties — which is precisely why Awal's column lands. The oldest sweet on the Diwali table is also the simplest, and it endures wherever one family member insists on making the trip to buy it.
